title: Neuron Firing (Action Potential)
description: Trace the complete action potential from resting state through depolarization to refractory period.
steps: Resting potential: neuron at -70mV baseline
Stimulus received at dendrites
Threshold reached at -55mV
Sodium channels open — rapid depolarization
Action potential travels down axon (saltatory conduction at nodes of Ranvier)
Signal reaches axon terminals
Refractory period: neuron resets
keyPrinciple: All-or-none principle: neuron fires completely or not at all.
frqRelevance: High — explain neural transmission in biological bases of behavior.

title: Synapse & Neurotransmission
description: Visualize the synaptic cleft with neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, and reuptake.
steps: Action potential arrives at presynaptic terminal
Synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitters into cleft
Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic gap
Bind to receptor sites on postsynaptic neuron
Signal continues (excitatory) or is blocked (inhibitory)
Reuptake: excess neurotransmitters reabsorbed by presynaptic neuron
keyPrinciple: Agonists mimic neurotransmitters; antagonists block receptors; reuptake inhibitors prevent reabsorption.
frqRelevance: High — drug mechanisms and neural communication.

title: Brain Region Map
description: Interactive brain profile showing the four lobes, cerebellum, brain stem, and limbic system with their functions.
steps: Frontal lobe: planning, decision-making, personality, speech production (Broca's area)
Parietal lobe: somatosensory processing, spatial awareness
Temporal lobe: auditory processing, speech comprehension (Wernicke's area), memory
Occipital lobe: visual processing
Cerebellum: balance, coordination, procedural learning
Brain stem (medulla & pons): breathing, heart rate, basic life functions
Limbic system: thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus, amygdala — emotion, memory, motivation
keyPrinciple: Damage to specific brain regions produces specific deficits. Broca's = speech production; Wernicke's = speech comprehension.
frqRelevance: High — brain structure-function relationships appear frequently.

title: Sleep Cycle & Stages
description: NREM stages 1-3 and REM sleep across a typical night, showing how REM frequency increases.
steps: Stage 1 (NREM): light sleep, hypnagogic sensations, theta waves
Stage 2 (NREM): sleep spindles and K-complexes, body temperature drops
Stage 3 (NREM): deep/slow-wave sleep, delta waves, hard to wake
REM sleep: paradoxical sleep — brain active like wakefulness, body paralyzed, dreaming occurs
Cycles repeat ~90 minutes each; REM periods get longer through the night
REM rebound: body compensates for REM deprivation with more REM next sleep
keyPrinciple: REM frequency increases as the sleep cycle progresses. Sleep disruptions affect physical and cognitive performance.
frqRelevance: Medium — EEG patterns and sleep stage identification.

title: Operant Conditioning Quadrant
description: The 2x2 matrix of positive/negative reinforcement and punishment with examples.
steps: Positive reinforcement: ADD desirable — behavior INCREASES
Negative reinforcement: REMOVE undesirable — behavior INCREASES
Positive punishment: ADD undesirable — behavior DECREASES
Negative punishment: REMOVE desirable — behavior DECREASES
frqRelevance: Very high — commonly tested with scenario-based questions.

title: Classical Conditioning Process
description: Trace the process from NS + UCS through acquisition to extinction and spontaneous recovery.
steps: Before conditioning: UCS → UCR (natural response). NS → no response.
During conditioning (acquisition): NS + UCS → UCR
After conditioning: CS → CR
Extinction: CS alone → CR fades
Spontaneous recovery: After rest, CS → CR reappears (weaker)
keyPrinciple: CS must come BEFORE UCS for successful acquisition. Spontaneous recovery applies to both classical and operant conditioning.
frqRelevance: Very high — scenario identification is a common exam question type.

title: Erikson's 8 Psychosocial Stages
description: Eight stages of psychosocial development across the lifespan, each with a core conflict.
steps: Trust vs Mistrust (infancy): Can I trust the world?
Autonomy vs Shame/Doubt (toddler): Can I do things myself?
Initiative vs Guilt (preschool): Is it okay for me to act?
Industry vs Inferiority (school age): Am I competent?
Identity vs Role Confusion (adolescence): Who am I?
Intimacy vs Isolation (young adult): Can I love and be loved?
Generativity vs Stagnation (middle adult): Am I contributing?
Integrity vs Despair (late adult): Was my life meaningful?
keyPrinciple: Each stage involves a psychosocial conflict that must be resolved. AP exam loves scenario-based Erikson questions.
frqRelevance: High — identify stage from behavior descriptions.

title: Normal Distribution & Standard Deviation
description: The bell curve showing mean, standard deviations, and the empirical rule percentages.
steps: Mean = Median = Mode (all at center)
68% of data within ±1 standard deviation
95% of data within ±2 standard deviations
99.7% of data within ±3 standard deviations
keyPrinciple: In a normal distribution, specific percentages of scores fall within each standard deviation from the mean.
frqRelevance: High — data interpretation on AAQ and MCQ.

title: Research Design Decision Tree
description: Flowchart for choosing the correct research method based on whether variables can be manipulated.
steps: Start: Can you manipulate a variable?
YES → Experiment (IV, DV, random assignment, control group)
NO → Which non-experimental method?
Case Study: in-depth single individual/group
Correlational: relationship between two variables (no causation)
Naturalistic Observation: observe in natural setting
Meta-Analysis: combine results from multiple studies
keyPrinciple: Only experiments establish cause and effect. Non-experimental methods cannot establish causation.
frqRelevance: Very high — research method identification appears on every exam.

title: Multi-Store Memory Model
description: The flow from sensory memory through short-term/working memory to long-term memory.
steps: Sensory memory: iconic (visual) and echoic (auditory) — very brief
Attention filters information to short-term memory
Short-term/working memory: limited capacity, temporary
Encoding (rehearsal, elaboration) transfers to long-term memory
Long-term memory: unlimited capacity, potentially permanent
Retrieval brings information back from long-term to working memory
keyPrinciple: Information must pass through each stage to be encoded correctly. Automatic processing happens without effort; effortful processing requires conscious attention.
frqRelevance: High — encoding strategies and memory failures.
